clue.text: England's safest pair of hands, perhaps, to trust when filling gin?

definitions.text: England's safest pair of hands, perhaps

indicators.note: one piece filling another means it is placed inside it

parts.note: Gordon's is a well-known brand of gin
to bank on someone is to trust them, so bank stands for trust

explanation.surface: A wry suggestion that England's most reliable goalkeeper is the man to rely on when topping up the gin.
explanation.walkthrough: Gordon Banks was England's goalkeeper in the 1966 World Cup win, famous for his safe hands; 'perhaps' marks him as one example.
explanation.definitionFit: A goalkeeper is the side's safest pair of hands, and Banks was England's most celebrated keeper.

clue.text: Virgilian poem snubbed last king in command

indicators.note: snubbed here means cut short, with the tail of the word lopped off

parts.note: George VI was the last King of Britain before the present reign
IC is the usual abbreviation for in command, i/c

explanation.surface: A literary note about a poem in which the last king was given the cold shoulder while in charge.
explanation.walkthrough: 'snubbed' looks like a social slight but means docked: GEORGE loses its last letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Virgil wrote the Georgics, four books of poetry about farming, so each is a Virgilian poem.

clue.text: Maybe Aga Khan's toe snagged by pet

indicators.note: a thing snagged by another is caught and held inside it

parts.note: a pet is a fit of sulky temper, a rage

indicators.note: the toe of a word is its foot or final letter

explanation.surface: The Aga Khan stubs a toe that gets caught by his pet animal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Aga Khan' looks like one name, but 'Maybe Aga' is the definition and 'Khan's toe' gives its last letter N for RAGE to catch.
explanation.definitionFit: An Aga is a brand of heavy cast-iron kitchen cooker, which is one kind of range.

clue.text: Divine location for exhibition centre

definitions.meaning: ... in Greece was the sanctuary of Zeus, a home of the gods' worship
A large exhibition hall in west London

explanation.surface: A sacred site recast as a venue for trade shows.
explanation.definitionFit: The same name serves the ancient Greek sanctuary of Zeus and the London events venue.

clue.text: Cynical Independent involved in Corbyn's downfall

indicators.note: being involved in something here means placed within it
a downfall brings the word crashing down into a new order

parts.note: the name Corbyn, with the possessive serving the surface
I is the standard abbreviation for Independent, as in politics

explanation.surface: A cynical independent politician had a hand in bringing down Jeremy Corbyn.
explanation.walkthrough: 'downfall' rearranges CORBYN as BYRONC, and 'involved in' puts I inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: Byronic suggests the brooding, disillusioned and sardonic manner of Lord Byron's heroes, hence world-weary and cynical.

clue.text: Stop-out partygoer hit Knightsbridge, spilling rum kegs

indicators.note: rum as an adjective means odd, signalling the letters are jumbled
spilling the letters of kegs means they leave the mix

parts.note: taken as written, letters to be removed

explanation.surface: A late-night reveller hits the bars of Knightsbridge and knocks over barrels of rum.
explanation.walkthrough: Take KNIGHTSBRIDGE, remove the letters of KEGS, and rearrange the rest (NIHTBRIDG). 'rum' looks like the drink but is the anagram signal; Knightsbridge is a smart London district.
explanation.definitionFit: A night bird is a person who stays out late, a stop-out who goes partying after dark.

clue.text: Alfresco effigy which will self-destruct in spring?

definitions.text: Alfresco effigy which will self-destruct in spring?

parts.words: Alfresco effigy which will self-destruct in spring?
parts.note: a figure built outdoors that melts away of its own accord when the weather warms

explanation.surface: An outdoor statue rigged to destroy itself when the season turns.
explanation.walkthrough: 'self-destruct' suggests a bomb or a spy gadget; it simply means melting in the spring thaw.
explanation.definitionFit: A figure made of packed snow stands outdoors in winter and melts as temperatures rise.

clue.text: 'U' is also confused with retro 'Y'

indicators.note: confused letters are mixed up into a new order
retro means looking backwards, so the letters are read in reverse

parts.note: Y stands for the yen, Japan's currency

explanation.surface: A puzzled remark about the letters U and Y being muddled with old-fashioned styling.
explanation.walkthrough: U is the old label for upper-class language and manners; Sloaney describes the posh Sloane Ranger set of west London.
explanation.definitionFit: Sloaney means typical of well-to-do Sloane Rangers, so suitably upper-class, which is what the label U means.

clue.text: Might this turn out like 'Instant' you initially ordered (one to go)?

definitions.text: Might this turn out like 'Instant' you initially ordered (one to go)?

indicators.note: ordered here means put into a new order, rearranged
one to go means that letter leaves the pool before rearranging
initially means take the first letter of the next word

parts.note: one is the Roman numeral I

explanation.surface: A coffee drinker wonders whether what they ordered to take away will come out tasting like instant.
explanation.walkthrough: Pool LIKE, INSTANT and Y, take out one I, then rearrange. 'to go' doubles as the coffee-shop phrase for takeaway.
explanation.definitionFit: A skinny latte is a coffee made with skimmed milk, the kind you order to go.

clue.text: Get back together on set

parts.note: re means on or about, as in a letter's heading
a set is a group of things or people

explanation.surface: An instruction to reunite on the film set.
explanation.definitionFit: To regroup is to reassemble or rally after being scattered.

clue.text: Fraud men chose, zip being possible outcome

indicators.note: a possible outcome of the letters is a different arrangement of them

explanation.surface: Men chose a fraud, and nothing at all was the likely result.
explanation.walkthrough: 'zip' looks like 'nothing', the natural result of a fraud, but it is simply fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: A Ponzi scheme is a swindle paying earlier investors with money from later ones.

clue.text: Fireplace where unmarried folk will strip

indicators.note: to strip something is to take off its outer layer, here both ends

parts.note: single people are singles

explanation.surface: A fireside spot where single people will take their clothes off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'strip' suggests undressing, but it removes the outer letters of SINGLES.
explanation.definitionFit: An ingle is an old word for a hearth or open fire, as in inglenook.

clue.text: Dock stalk on plant

parts.note: a pen is a sheltered dock, as for submarines
a stem is a plant's stalk

explanation.surface: A gardening note about the stalk of a dock plant.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dock' looks like the weed, a plant itself, but it is a dock for boats.
explanation.definitionFit: Penstemon is a garden perennial with tubular flowers, sometimes called beardtongue.

clue.text: Capital I invested in dodgy casino

indicators.note: something invested in another is put inside it
dodgy means unsound, signalling the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A confession of having put money into a shady gambling house.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Capital' and 'invested' sound like money, but the capital is a city.
explanation.definitionFit: Nicosia is the capital city of Cyprus.

clue.text: Horrid chant about writer's insides

indicators.note: about means going round, so one piece wraps the other

parts.note: to chant is to sing

indicators.note: the insides of a word are all but its first and last letters

parts.note: the writer is Charles Dickens

explanation.surface: An unpleasant chant that goes on about an author's guts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'insides' reads like guts, the horrid image, but it keeps only the middle of the writer's name, and 'about' wraps the chant round that.
explanation.definitionFit: Sickening means nauseating or revolting, a strong synonym for horrid.

clue.text: EU character not in favour of another's wine

parts.note: chi is a letter of the Greek alphabet, and Greece is in the EU
anti means against

explanation.surface: Someone in the European Union dislikes a foreign country's wine.
explanation.walkthrough: The Greek letter comes from one EU member, the wine from another: Italy.
explanation.definitionFit: Chianti is a red wine from Tuscany, so the wine of Italy, another EU country.

clue.text: Say Hutton's better being cover

parts.note: Len Hutton, for example, is a Hutton, so Hutton's is Len's
to cap is to better or outdo

explanation.surface: A claim that the cricketer Hutton's performance was finer as cover.
explanation.walkthrough: Len Hutton was an England opening batsman of the 1930s to 1950s; 'cover' looks like the cricket fielding position but is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A lens cap is the protective lid that covers a camera lens.

clue.text: Goes through three stacks of chalk

definitions.meaning: to needle is to pierce or pass through, as a needle does
three chalk sea stacks off the Isle of Wight

explanation.surface: Someone working through three piles of chalk.
explanation.definitionFit: The verb sense is piercing like a needle; the noun is the rock formation off the English south coast.

clue.text: Rank European polymaths: ____ has to appear

definitions.text: Rank European polymaths: ____ has to appear

indicators.note: rank means foul or corrupted, signalling a rearrangement
has has to appear beside the blank, so its letters are the leftovers of the mix

explanation.surface: Listing European polymaths, a name in the blank must be included.
explanation.walkthrough: E plus POLYMATHS rearranges to the blank plus HAS; the blank is filled by one of the polymaths.
explanation.definitionFit: Ptolemy, the Alexandrian astronomer, geographer and mathematician, is one of history's great polymaths.

clue.text: Perfectly hit Chopin's first note

parts.note: to middle a ball is to strike it perfectly with the sweet spot

indicators.note: first means take the opening letter of the next word

explanation.surface: Praise for a pianist striking Chopin's opening note flawlessly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'middle' as a verb is a sports term for hitting the ball cleanly in the centre of the bat.
explanation.definitionFit: Middle C is the note near the centre of the piano keyboard.

clue.text: 'Zine on web covering oxygen generator

indicators.note: in a down clue on means placed above the next piece
in a down clue covering means sitting on top of what follows

parts.note: a zine is a magazine, a mag
a web is a net
O is the chemical symbol for oxygen

explanation.surface: An online fanzine reports on an oxygen generating machine.
explanation.definitionFit: A magneto is a small electrical generator using permanent magnets, as in an engine's ignition.

clue.text: Chapstick aggravated blip over a large mass

indicators.note: in a down clue over means the first part sits above the rest
aggravated means stirred up, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: M is the symbol for mass

explanation.surface: A lip balm stick made worse by a blip over a big lump.
explanation.definitionFit: Chapstick is a brand of lip salve, used generically for a soothing balm for lips.

clue.text: Track particle drunk by the gallon

indicators.note: something drunk by another is taken inside it

parts.note: a meson is a subatomic particle

explanation.surface: A tiny particle is downed by the gallon.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Track' looks like a path but is a recorded piece of music.
explanation.definitionFit: A theme song is a musical track associated with a film or programme.

clue.text: Close to border, leaving body in bushes

indicators.note: a letter leaving a word is taken out of it

parts.note: a corpse is a dead body

indicators.note: the close of a word is its last letter

explanation.surface: A body has been dumped in the bushes near the frontier.
explanation.definitionFit: A copse is a small thicket of trees and undergrowth, a clump of shrubs and bushes.

clue.text: Plan of Winston's home not showing well

indicators.note: a part not showing is left out of the word

parts.note: Chartwell in Kent was Winston Churchill's country house

explanation.surface: A design for Churchill's house that looks unwell.
explanation.walkthrough: Chartwell, Churchill's home in Kent, loses WELL; 'not showing well' looks like being off-colour.
explanation.definitionFit: A chart is a map or diagram, a plan.

clue.text: Devious doubling of perimeters around emotional President?

indicators.note: one piece placed around another wraps it
the perimeters of a word are its outside letters
doubling means the same pair is used a second time

parts.note: Ike was the nickname of US President Eisenhower

explanation.surface: Twice circling the edges of a tearful president, in a devious way.
explanation.walkthrough: The outer letters E and L of 'emotional' go around another copy of themselves for EELL, then IKE follows.
explanation.definitionFit: An eel is slippery and hard to hold, so eel-like means evasive and devious.

clue.text: Asian food crop returns earned before twelve Eastern

indicators.note: returns means the word goes back, read the other way

parts.note: earned means made, as in made money
AM means before noon

explanation.surface: A crop in Asia makes a profit in the morning out east.
explanation.definitionFit: Edamame are young green soybeans, a crop eaten in Japanese and other Asian cooking.

clue.text: Add two thirds of egg into bean-flavoured buns to create baker's nightmare?

indicators.note: a piece put into another goes inside it

parts.note: soy is the bean, used as flavouring

indicators.note: two of the three letters, here the last pair

parts.note: buns is slang for buttocks, the bottom

explanation.surface: A recipe instruction to add egg to soya buns, ending in baking disaster.
explanation.walkthrough: 'buns' looks like baking but is slang for the backside. A soggy bottom is pastry left undercooked underneath, a famous fault on TV's Great British Bake Off.
explanation.definitionFit: Undercooked pastry with a damp base is what every baker dreads, hence a nightmare.
